Making SŌKAI
A making-of · Blender 5.2 · Cycles · Three.js r186

Making SŌKAI, from sketch to living sword

How the Infinite edition was built in one session: a katana modeled from real cross-sections in Blender, two worlds lit by path tracing and baked into textures, then brought to life in the browser with live materials, weather and a draw-and-cut. Each step below animates the process, then shows what it actually produced.

蒼
Process
01 / 11

The process, in writing

  1. Diagnose, then set the target

    The earlier versions looked worse than the concept art because the geometry was primitive and the materials were flat. So the two concept images became the strict reference (black urushi saya with a cobalt-to-cyan streak, silver fittings, cobalt ito over ivory samegawa, a night atelier opening onto a garden with a ring of light), and the brief became: real geometry, real light, fewer and better things.

  2. Model the blade from cross-sections

    A shinogi-zukuri profile (edge, hira-ji, shinogi ridge, shinogi-ji, peaked iori-mune) is lofted along an arc of 3.5 m radius, which gives an 18 mm sori over a 710 mm blade. Width tapers from 31.5 to 21.8 mm and thickness from 7.2 to 5.0 mm; in the last 34 mm the edge curves up into the kissaki (fukura) and the ridge becomes the ko-shinogi. Ridges are marked sharp so light breaks cleanly along them. The tang, habaki and seppa are separate objects.

  3. Wrap the handle for real

    The tsuka is a slightly waisted oval core under a samegawa shell. Four silk ribbons follow helices with a 51.2 mm pitch, two in each direction, so they cross on both faces every 25.6 mm and alternate over and under. The gaps between them are true diamond openings, which is why the ivory samegawa shows through. The ∞ menuki sit half under the wrap.

  4. Cut the tsuba with Booleans

    Each guard starts as a solid iron plate. Cutter shapes (the nakago hole, two teardrops inside a lemniscate, crescent moons; or five sakura petals; or a moon and three waves) are subtracted with Blender's exact Boolean solver, then bevelled so the edges catch light. A raised rim and gilt inlay bands are separate geometry. Three designs were built and ray-tested to confirm every opening goes through.

  5. Build the saya, fittings and sageo

    The saya is lofted from superellipse sections along the same arc, with a real mouth opening and a dark interior for when the blade is drawn. Koiguchi, kojiri, kurigata and a flat braided sageo wound four times with metal-tipped tails complete the mounting: eighteen parts in all.

  6. Model two worlds

    The atelier is built from about 600 procedural objects: individual floor planks, timber frame, sliding shoji with kumiko lattice, a forge with coals, andon lanterns, a carved katana-kake with a mon crest, an indigo cloth, a vase of sakura. Through the open screens: a pond, an arched bridge, stone lanterns, a rock waterfall, pines, and the cyan ring portal. The vault beyond the ring is a stepped plinth, an avenue of memory monoliths and a monumental ring.

  7. Light it in Cycles and bake the light

    All static geometry is merged, unwrapped into one shared UV atlas and path-traced in Cycles on the Apple M5 GPU at 768 samples, baking a 4096 × 4096 lightmap per lighting state (night and dawn, 124 to 146 seconds each). Merging before baking was the key optimisation: baking 559 objects one by one took about 75 times longer. Emissive lamps, water, blossoms and pine needles stay out of the bake so they can move and change with the seasons.

  8. Capture reflections from the sword's own position

    Cycles also renders an equirectangular HDR panorama from where the katana sits, one per lighting state. In the browser it is prefiltered into mip levels so polished steel, lacquer and silver reflect the actual room. Very bright pixels (candle flames) are compressed first, which removed sparkle artefacts along the hamon.

  9. Export and generate materials live

    The katana and worlds export as one meshopt-compressed GLB with named parts. In the browser, the hamon (five styles), steel roughness, lacquer with its streak, raden flecks and maki-e pattern, braided silk, samegawa nodules, hammered iron and engraved scrollwork are generated as textures on a canvas, so every choice in the Forge is live.

  10. Add light, atmosphere and weather

    A render pipeline adds wet-floor and pond reflections, soft shadows from a spot light, bloom on the emissive lamps, depth of field when close, a film grade and grain. The sky, stars, clouds, mist, moonbeams, dust, forge sparks, rain, snow, petals, maple leaves and fireflies are all generated in shaders. Seasons recolour the foliage; weather changes the fog, wetness and grade; lightning flashes the baked light.

  11. Make it interactive and make it remember

    Orbit and zoom toward the cursor, hover to name any part, double-click to fly to it. Pull the handle and the blade slides along the sori arc; explode it into its eighteen parts; press Iai for a draw, a diagonal cut with a light trail, chiburi and a slow return to the scabbard. Settings, the last view and a named collection of forgings are saved in the browser. Finally, everything is packed into one self-contained HTML file of about 13 MB.

Outputs along the way

An artistic reconstruction, not a scan, historical certification or fabrication guide. The theme is an original homage inspired by the film Infinite (2021); no material from the film is used. Frames on this page were captured from the running app and from Blender.
